articles.fullText:
The polling dates for the 2027 Rural Ordinary Election were published in the Government Gazette today.

The Village Representative Election will be conducted on January 17, 2027, while the Kaifong Representative Election for Market Towns will be held on January 24, 2027. The nomination period will take place from November 24 to December 7.

The election covers 709 recognised villages with a total of 1,484 representative seats. These comprise 695 resident representative seats and 789 indigenous inhabitant representative seats. Separately, the market towns on Cheung Chau and Peng Chau will elect 39 and 17 neighbourhood (“kaifong”) representatives respectively.

​A notice specifying the polling date, time and polling station address will be issued to eligible electors at least 10 days before the polling day.

Call 2152 1521 or contact the relevant New Territories district office for enquiries.

articles.title: Economy rises 5.2% in Q3
articles.excerpt: (To watch the full press conference with sign language interpretation, click here .) Underpinned by a further pick-up in external…
articles.fullText:
(To watch the full press conference with sign language interpretation, click here .)

Underpinned by a further pick-up in external trade growth and solid domestic demand, Hong Kong's economy expanded strongly in the third quarter of 2026, with real gross domestic product (GDP) rising 5.2% year on year.

Presenting the Third Quarter Economic Report 2026 at a press conference today, Government Economist Irina Fan said that in the first three quarters, real GDP grew by 5.1% over a year earlier, which is the fastest pace in five years for the corresponding period.

Total goods exports surged 30.3% year on year in the third quarter, fueled by strong global demand for artificial intelligence-related electronics.

Domestically, private consumption rose 2.9% for its sixth consecutive quarter of growth.

Factoring in the results from the first three quarters and expectations of continued solid growth in the fourth, the full-year GDP growth forecast for 2026 has been revised up to 4.8%.

Looking ahead, Ms Fan said that, supported by robust global AI investment and related trade, Hong Kong's economy is poised for a strong full-year performance.

“Incoming data for entering the fourth quarter also points to sustained growth momentum. Domestic demand should stay resilient. However, uncertainty in the external environment persists, including those from geopolitical tensions, US monetary policy, and trade protectionist measures. So, all of these are worth closer monitoring.”

She noted that the overall inflation rate should remain moderate.

Taking into account inflation in the first three quarters, the forecasts for the underlying and headline consumer price inflation rates for 2026 have been revised down to 1.9% and 2.0% respectively.

articles.title: Jensen Huang steps down as Nvidia CEO
articles.excerpt: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the AI industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of…
articles.fullText:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the AI industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of the chipmaker he built into an AI powerhouse.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the company said on Thursday.

It named former Synopsys CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 percent, will exit the board as well.

Nvidia shares fell more than 10 percent in premarket trading, and weighed on the broader market.

Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.

China has dismissed the spying allegations, calling them "baseless".

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to consider his ouster, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that Huang also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

Huang's exit plunges the US$4 trillion company into uncertainty and threatens to disrupt an AI ecosystem that he helped bankroll by pouring Nvidia's swelling cash pile back into cloud providers, suppliers and the industry's biggest labs.

"The risk is not that Nvidia suddenly loses its technology roadmap... that roadmap is largely visible for the next several years. The risk is execution. Jensen has been the chief conductor of an extraordinarily complex system," said Michael Feldman, portfolio manager at ClearBridge Investments.

"In a world with real bottlenecks, that coordination is a competitive advantage in itself."

Investor sentiment toward AI stocks has already been shaky as soaring cash burn and rising debt at traditionally cash-rich tech giants fuel doubts over whether the AI boom will pay off. (Reuters)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: The Download: COP31’s climate challenge and the quest for immortality
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

What to know about this year’s UN climate talks

Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists have gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual UN climate talks. But this year’s negotiations are taking place against a particularly tense geopolitical backdrop, as the world falls further behind the Paris Agreement’s goals.

Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action.

Here’s what you need to know about COP31 . 

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Inside the quest for cognitive immortality

Far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going beyond death. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores their ideas, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud.

Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion.

Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST .

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang
The board will meet as soon as today to determine his future. ( WSJ $)
+ Nvidia’s stock slid 8% after the report was published. ( BI )
+ Huang allegedly also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague. ( NYT $)
+ His exit could send shockwaves across the AI industry. ( Axios )
+ Stakes are high in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 The Nvidia spy scandal is set to tighten chip exports
But Commerce Secretary Lutnick has stalled the curbs. ( CNBC )
+ China has signaled it will retaliate if they pass. ( FT $)
+ Chinese firms have started stockpiling Nvidia chips. ( Reuters $)
+ Democrats appear to be preparing an investigation. ( Politico )

3 A startup has built an AI to detect AI-made bioweapons
It runs offline on a laptop with a USB gene sequencer. ( Wired $)
+ Ukraine is opening up its battlefield data to train AI weapons. ( NYT $)
+ AI is making bioweapons easier to create. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Anduril says its satellite can track spacecraft in orbital night
It uses an infrared sensor to detect hidden satellites. ( Ars Technica )
+ Anduril is also making smart glasses for warfare. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Ukraine has reported new restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield
Zelenskyy says they’re hampering drone defenses. ( NBC News

6 Even remote Brazilian wildlife has microplastics in its blood
Animals 100 km from waste sites carried them. ( Nature )
+ AstroTurf is increasing microplastic levels. ( MIT Technology Review )

7 A NASA space camera can spot invasive plants from orbit
It detects how different species’ leaves reflect light. ( Economist $)

8 Astronomers have found an “invisible” object that defies stellar theory
It’s likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star. ( 404 Media )
+ New research has corroborated the first black hole image. ( New Scientist $)

9 Life may have started with metabolism, not genes
Self-sustaining chemical cycles could have come first. ( Quanta )

10 Brain surgery has left a man seeing cat eyes on people
Researchers used AI to render what he sees. ( Gizmodo )

Quote of the day

“I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products—are essentially progressive.”

—Alex Karp, Palantir’s CEO, tells Politico that he’s a devoted Democrat despite recently backing Trump.

One more thing

How Chinese short dramas became AI content machines

China’s short drama industry is fueled by bite-sized, melodramatic, and smutty shows built for smartphone scrolling. Now, many are being made entirely with AI: no actors, camera operators, cinematographers, or CGI specialists required.

An average of 470 AI-generated short dramas were released every day in January. Production timelines have shrunk from months to weeks, while costs have dropped by up to 90%. Storytelling is also increasingly driven by performance data.

The format is rapidly expanding overseas while reshaping the work of writers and production crews. Read the full story on AI’s dramatic impact on China’s short drama industry .

—Caiwei Chen

We can still have nice things

articles.title: Carrick sacked by Man U, Sage out as Palace manager
articles.excerpt: Manchester United have dismissed manager Michael Carrick, the club said on Thursday, after a prolonged winless Premier League run culminated…
articles.fullText:
Manchester United have dismissed manager Michael Carrick, the club said on Thursday, after a prolonged winless Premier League run culminated in a 4-4 draw at home to Aston Villa last weekend, leaving the team mired in the relegation zone.

United have won only three of their 15 matches in all competitions under Carrick this season – including one league victory – leaving them 18th in the table on eight points after 10 games, one point from the bottom.

"After a disappointing start to the season, the club has come to the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions," United said in a statement on their website.

Carrick came under mounting pressure after a 3-0 home loss to Bournemouth and the former United midfielder carried the air of someone awaiting the inevitable after the defeat when fans chanted his name but booed the players off the pitch.

He had dropped captain Bruno Fernandes to the bench against Bournemouth and did not bring him on even when United were desperate for inspiration in midfield, but the struggling club gave Carrick another chance to revive their season.

Although he restored the playmaker to the starting lineup against Chelsea following clear-the-air talks and spoke of the team's determination to put things right, little changed as they were comprehensively outplayed in a 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge.

A 3-2 comeback win over AS Roma in the Champions League briefly eased the pressure on Carrick, but United's familiar defensive frailties were exposed again in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, despite two injury-time goals salvaging a point.

Carrick is likely to be replaced by Mauricio Pochettino, the US men's national team coach, who has agreed to take over the newly-vacant post, according to reports in British media.

The former Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea manager is one of the Premier League's most highly regarded former coaches.

Another struggling Premier League side, Crystal Palace, have also fired their manager.

Pierre Sage was let go on Thursday, bringing the Frenchman's five-month tenure to an end after a poor start to the season left the club bottom of the table.

Sage's departure followed a 3-1 home loss to Liverpool on Sunday, the south London club's fourth straight Premier League defeat. They are two points outside the safety zone.

"Crystal Palace Football Club can confirm that Pierre Sage has left his role as manager," Palace said in a statement.

"Three members of Pierre’s coaching staff – Jamal Alioui, Damien Della Santa and Sandy Guichard – have also left the club."

The 47-year-old, who managed Ligue 1 sides RC Lens and Olympique Lyonnais, took charge at Selhurst Park in June.

British media reports said former Tottenham Hotspur and Brentford manager Thomas Frank is the leading candidate to replace Sage. (Reuters)
_____________________________
Last updated: 2026-11-12 HKT 21:29

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: 'US uses spying claims as pretext for tech blockade'
articles.excerpt: China accused the United States on Thursday of using spurious spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade"…
articles.fullText:
China accused the United States on Thursday of using spurious spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on Beijing, following claims that Nvidia boss Jensen Huang was the victim of a Chinese espionage plot.

"China's technological progress is driven by independent innovation and open cooperation. The US side should stop fabricating such 'spy' narratives as a pretext for imposing a technological blockade," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and turned it into the world's leading supplier of the chips that power AI, has admitted to having an extramarital affair.

China has dismissed the claims about spying on Huang as "groundless speculation" and "an attempt to smear China".

The furore comes ahead of a meeting next week between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump at the Apec summit in Shenzhen. (AFP)

Edited by Edmond Fong

articles.title: HK, region take toll as Nvidia fate hangs in balance
articles.excerpt: Asian shares and US futures declined on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks…
articles.fullText:
Asian shares and US futures declined on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index closed down 307 points, or 1.3 percent, to 24,008 on turnover of HK$202.65 billion.

The tech index plunged 95 points, or 2.4 percent, to 3,931 while the China enterprises index fell 114 points, or 1.4 percent, to 8,056.

Up north, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index ended down 24 points, or 0.67 percent, at 3,655.

The Shenzhen Component Index fell 191 points, or 1.68 percent, to 11,197 while the ChiNext Index dived 62 points, or 2.44 percent, to 2,509.

In after-hours trading, Nvidia’s shares fell 8.6 percent after reports said Nvidia’s board was meeting late on Wednesday to discuss the situation surrounding its chief executive, Jensen Huang and his extramarital affairs.

Nvidia's shares climbed 2.9 percent on Wednesday.

Its shares have fallen after the company said it was investigating Huang, who has admitted to being unfaithful to his wife.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang was involved in a second extramarital affair.

The tech company's board was preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang's future, according to the Wall Street Journal, which quoted people familiar with the matter.

Huang has built Nvidia to be one of the world's biggest and most important companies, designing advanced chips crucial to the AI buildout that has helped drive stock markets to record highs and boosted economies around the world.

"Nvidia has spent years convincing investors that it is one of the most important companies in the AI revolution," wrote Charu Chanana at Saxo Markets.

"Now, the biggest question surrounding the company is not about its chips, competitors or earnings. It is about its founder."

She said Huang was key to the firm's future, including dealings with governments.

"Nvidia's technological advantage would not disappear with his departure," she added.

"Its CUDA software ecosystem, product capabilities and customer relationships remain formidable strengths.

"But an abrupt exit without a credible succession plan could force investors to reassess how much of Nvidia's future depends on Huang personally."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei reversed early gains to end 429 points, or 0.7 percent, lower at 60,819 amid reports that a potential sacking was in the offing at Nvidia for its founder, Jensen Huang.

The broader Topix edged up almost eight points, or 0.2 percent, at 3,937.

In Seoul, the Nvidia reports also took its toll on the Kospi, sending it down 32 points, or 0.61 percent, to 5,342. (Agencies)

Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Apec to spotlight Shenzhen's global fintech push
articles.excerpt: Shenzhen’s financial services sector has been increasingly shaped by the deep integration of fintech and by its expanding overseas reach…
articles.fullText:
Shenzhen’s financial services sector has been increasingly shaped by the deep integration of fintech and by its expanding overseas reach, according to a senior executive at Ping An Property and Casualty Insurance Company.

Those trends are likely to draw wider attention next week, when global leaders arrive in the southern Chinese city for the Apec summit.

Xu Hua, assistant president of Ping An Property and Casualty Insurance Company, said the company’s own history mirrors Shenzhen's fintech development.

Founded in the 1980s in Shekou – an industrial area in western Shenzhen – it has grown from a regional insurer into a service network covering more than 110 countries.

Financial services already form one of Shenzhen’s four pillar industries. Ping An Property and Casualty Insurance Company is among the companies taking part in the meeting, and its parent, Ping An Group, is one of the official sponsors.

Xu said Shenzhen’s financial industry is most characterised by the deep integration of finance and technology.

"Shenzhen is an innovation capital. It brings together a group of representative technology companies. Technological innovation comes with trial and error and risk. It faces practical difficulties such as high research and development investment, rapid technology iteration and strong uncertainty," he said.

"Wherever innovation goes, insurance must follow. Overall, technology is Shenzhen’s underlying character. What insurance needs to do is serve well as a shock absorber for the real economy, so that technology companies dare to innovate, dare to invest and dare to go global."

Xu said the company has tailor-made more than 400 million yuan in dedicated risk protection for this summit.

He believes the meeting will not only bring short-term benefits, but also have long-term value, and hopes that the exchange opportunities at the Apec meeting can be transformed into sustained project cooperation.

For cross-border operations, he called for closer cooperation with insurers, reinsurers and professional service providers so that companies can better understand local risks and coverage requirements.

In sectors such as new energy, advanced manufacturing and the digital economy, he proposed that industry partners jointly assess emerging risks and develop products that keep pace with innovation.

Xu said that in addition to helping mainland enterprises go global and providing protection services for their overseas expansion, the company has also formed close ties with Apec economies.

The sector’s scale underscores its role in the city: financial services account for nearly 15 percent of Shenzhen’s GDP, and the Shenzhen Stock Exchange had more than 2,900 listed companies as of the end of September.

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: HK, region mixed as Nvidia faces crunch on Huang sack
articles.excerpt: Asian stocks wobbled at the start of regional trading on Thursday, while Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading on news…
articles.fullText:
Asian stocks wobbled at the start of regional trading on Thursday, while Nvidia shares plunged in after-hours trading on news that its board may oust longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

In Hong Kong, the benchmark Hang Seng Index opened down 194 points, or 0.8 percent, at 24,121.

The tech index fell 32 points, or 0.8 percent, to 3,995 while the China Enterprises Index slipped 66 points, or 0.81 percent, to 8,105.

On the mainland, the Shanghai Composite Index inched down seven points, or 0.21 percent, to open at 3,673.

The Shenzhen Component Index was 28 points, or 0.25 percent, lower at 11,361 while the ChiNext Index was down 0.5 percent at 2,559.

Nvidia's board is meeting late on Wednesday to decide whether to oust Huang, a source said, as the world's dominant supplier of AI processors grapples with the fallout of allegations that he had an affair with a suspected spy for China.

The New York Times has also reported that Huang had had an affair with a company executive who reported to him.

"It looks bad from every single angle," said Jake Dollarhide, chief executive at Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

"I believe the board won't oust him until they have an all-star, a known entity in the tech sector, to replace him. At the end of the day, let's not forget that the Nvidia chip is the centrepiece of the AI story."

Shares in Nvidia slid more than eight percent after the bell, weighing on S&P 500 e-mini futures, which slipped 0.4 percent.

In Tokyo, the Nikkei opened 226 points, or 0.37 percent, higher at 61,475 and was 390 points higher still at one stage before noon.

In Seoul, the Kospi opened 10 points, or 0.2 percent, at 5,385 and, like the Nikkei, tracked up cautiously by 38 points at one stage before lunch.

"Renewed optimism around AI drove US equities higher overnight, with positive developments around CoreWeave and Anthropic adding to enthusiasm around the sector and helping the S&P 500 and Nasdaq rally," Westpac analysts wrote in a note. (Agencies)

Edited by Aaron Tam

articles.title: Andreeva stuns Sabalenka to reach WTA Finals last four
articles.excerpt: French Open champion Mirra Andreeva stormed past Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to reach the last four of the WTA Finals…
articles.fullText:
French Open champion Mirra Andreeva stormed past Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 6-0 to reach the last four of the WTA Finals on Wednesday as Elina Svitolina kept her bid on track with a three-set win over Karolina Muchova.

Russian 19-year-old Andreeva held her nerve after falling behind 4-1 in the opening set, winning the last 11 games to seal the round-robin victory in just 62 minutes.

"Oh my God, I'm even happier than I was after my first match," Andreeva said. "I feel like I can play another two matches, I'm so full of energy. I'm so pumped up. I'm so happy."

Andreeva, whose three titles this year include her maiden major at Roland Garros, is making her singles debut in the elite season-ending event.

The world number three seemed to be feeling the nerves in the early going against second-ranked Sabalenka.

Irked that she had given up a break with a double fault, she was able to flip the switch, dealing handily with Sabalenka's big serves and pushing the Belarusian star back with her own big groundstrokes.

Andreeva crucially kept momentum on her side with a break for a 3-0 lead in the second set.

Sabalenka, trailing 0-40, saved three break points, but Andreeva gave herself another with a swinging volley winner and grabbed another break when a Sabalenka forehand flew just long.

The increasingly demoralised Sabalenka had no answer. After the Belarusian smacked a backhand into the net to give her opponent match point Andreeva polished things off with a service winner.

It was another disappointing performance for the 28-year-old Sabalenka, whose three wins this season include prestigious back-to-back victories at Indian Wells and Miami but no Grand Slams.

Making her sixth straight Finals appearance, Sabalenka can still advance if she beats Svitolina in their final round-robin match on Friday.

Svitolina roared back from a set down to beat Muchova 3-6, 6-2, 6-2.

Ukrainian veteran Svitolina lifted the WTA Finals trophy in 2018 but hadn't been back to the elite season-ending event since 2019.

She got off to a rocky start against Muchova, who broke Svitolina three times in the opening set.

Trailing 2-1 on serve in the second Svitolina found her range, winning five straight games to force a third set.

"I was not happy with the first set," Svitolina said. "I didn't play as well. I just made some adjustments, tactical adjustments.

"I think it helped me also to be more aggressive, because I was too passive in the first set," Svitolina said.

Muchova's second round-robin defeat coupled with Andreeva's victory means the Czech was eliminated from semi-final contention. (AFP)

Edited by Nazvi Careem

articles.title: Nvidia preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang: WSJ
articles.excerpt: Nvidia's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after he had two extramarital affairs, the Wall Street Journal reported…
articles.fullText:
Nvidia's board is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after he had two extramarital affairs, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The board is preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to determine his future, the report added.

Huang's potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly US$4 trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the dominant supplier of AI chips at the centre of the global artificial-intelligence boom.

The company's shares slid about 8 percent in after-hours trading. Including Wednesday's after-hours selloff, Nvidia has lost about US$600 billion in stock market value this week since the board announced its investigation.

"Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place... If Mr Huang broke the law or violated company policies, the board is likely to act as soon as they have proof," Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson, said.

Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.

The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five people who worked at the company.

When reached by phone on Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Powell, Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly." He then hung up, the New York Times reported.

Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the reports.

The reports mark a sharp escalation in a controversy that began with revelations about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence has said was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

Beijing has dismissed allegations that Alice Huang was a spy for China as "groundless speculation".

In a memo to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility," but gave no details about the relationship.

The same day, Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The probe is being overseen by independent directors with outside legal counsel. At the time, the board expressed confidence in Huang.

US President Donald Trump has said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang but voiced support for the Nvidia chief, calling him "an honourable guy" who had "done an amazing job for our country."

Huang faces a potential congressional subpoena if he doesn't respond to a request to provide a closed-door briefing about the allegations that he had a close relationship with the Chinese businesswoman.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 with Curtis Priem and Chris Malachowsky. Its early hits were graphics chips for computer games, before its CUDA software opened the processors to general computing and, later, AI. (Reuters)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: CoreWeave results lift tech stocks as dollar gains
articles.excerpt: Stock markets rose on Wednesday on renewed optimism over AI following strong results from data centre operator CoreWeave, while the…
articles.fullText:
Stock markets rose on Wednesday on renewed optimism over AI following strong results from data centre operator CoreWeave, while the dollar extended a rally on expectations for at least one more Federal Reserve interest rate hike.

Wall Street's main indices enjoyed a buoyant session led by the tech-heavy Nasdaq, which finished up 1.6 percent.

"The primary catalyst for the upside action is, ironically, one of the primary catalysts for the downside action that had been seen in the AI trade," said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare.

"That would be CoreWeave, which posted better-than-feared third-quarter results and issued a reassuring outlook that has quieted some of the debt financing concerns surrounding its AI buildout plans," he added.

CoreWeave said sales would come in at US$13-US$13.3 billion this year, beating estimates and soothing worries about its ability to finance its heavy debt burden, which fuelled a sharp sell-off last month.

Shares in CoreWeave surged nearly 25 percent.

"This relief trade is carrying across the AI trade complex to include hardware, software, and semiconductor stocks," said O'Hare.

The gains in US equities came despite signalling from US central bankers that the Fed will lift interest rates in December to address persistent inflation. The US dollar rose to its highest level since May 2025 after one top Fed official floated the idea of a 0.5 percentage point interest rate increase next month.

After last week's rout fuelled by fears that Democrats would ramp up regulation of AI, tech stocks have bounced this week on bargain-buying and hopes that fears may have been overdone.

"Overall, the market is putting AI doubts to one side and is focusing on revenue potential and mega cap IPO as we move through this week," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

Semiconductor companies advanced, including scandal-plagued Nvidia, which bounced 3 percent after a two-day rout following the bombshell revelation of an affair between CEO Jensen Huang and a woman suspected of being a spy. The firm is now the subject of an FBI investigation.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 254 points, or 0.5 percent, to 52,486, the S&P 500 gained 98 points, or 1.3 percent, to 7,619 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 400 points, or 1.6percent, to 25,466.

Oil prices advanced after sinking on Tuesday on hopes for a US-Iran agreement to end their war and reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz. (AFP)

Edited by Cecil Wong

articles.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
articles.excerpt: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks…
articles.fullText:
It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

articles.title: Teacher certificate bill proposed
articles.excerpt: The Education Bureau has proposed amending the law to enhance the teacher registration mechanism by introducing practising certificate requirements, thereby…
articles.fullText:
The Education Bureau has proposed amending the law to enhance the teacher registration mechanism by introducing practising certificate requirements, thereby upholding the professionalism of the teaching force. The Government will publish the Education (Amendment) Bill 2026 in the Gazette tomorrow and introduce it to the Legislative Council for first and second readings on November 25.

The bureau noted that it has referenced teacher registration systems in various jurisdictions alongside the registration and practising certificate requirements of other Hong Kong professions. It stated that making a practising certificate a prerequisite for teaching, in addition to the existing statutory registration, could elevate public recognition of the sector and raise the social status of teachers.

The bill will establish statutory rules requiring all teachers and principals of publicly funded schools, private schools, international schools and kindergartens to hold both teacher registration and practising certificates. Each practising certificate will remain valid for a maximum of three school years.

To ensure educators keep abreast of the latest global and local educational policies, teachers must meet a mandatory continuing professional development requirement to obtain a practising certificate. This measure aims to align their knowledge and pedagogy with the evolving needs of students and society.

The bureau pointed out that as role models and key figures in nurturing young people, teachers have a profound impact on students through their conduct, values, words and deeds. Amid rapid societal changes, parents and the wider public hold increasingly high expectations for teacher professionalism.

The bureau highlighted that the bill addresses the practical operational needs of schools, encourages educators to keep pace with the times and strengthens staff management to safeguard student well-being. It also establishes safeguards to bar individuals convicted of offences endangering national security from teaching, protecting students while upholding professional integrity and public confidence.

articles.title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind

As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud.

Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be .

—Antonio Regalado

This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?

Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.

The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems .

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking
Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. ( Politico )
+ It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. ( New Scientist $)
+ John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. ( Guardian )
+ But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. ( NYT $)
+ What’s the future of electricity? ( MIT Technology Review )

2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips
Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. ( Information $)
+ Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One . ( NYT $)
+ Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. ( Verge )
+ Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. ( Reuters $)

3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible”
Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. ( NYT $)
+ This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion
It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. ( Guardian )

5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data
Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. ( Reuters $)
+ Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. ( Ars Technica )

6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people
The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. ( FT $)
+ Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. ( SCMP )

7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades
One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. ( Wired $)
+ “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz
AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. ( BBC )

9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble
That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. ( Quanta )

10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here’s what it’s taught us
Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. ( New Scientist $)

Quote of the day

“What a dereliction of duty. He’s supposed to protect America, not China, not his friends.”

—Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy.

One more thing

How refrigeration ruined fresh food

Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus.

According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.

Read the full story on her research .

—Allison Arieff

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world.
+ Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos .
+ Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year.
+ Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael’s “Careless Whisper.”

articles.title: North Korean affordability crisis: monthly salary can’t buy even a bag of rice
articles.excerpt: Workers start every month deep in the red as inflation guts official wages and forces reliance on side hustles.
articles.fullText:
[Editor's Note] To protect the safety of sources inside North Korea who could face severe punishment by authorities if identified, the family featured in this article is a composite model based on reporting from exclusive interviews conducted by RFA Korean journalists with two separate households inside North Korea. One household is a couple working at a state-run factory who shared their wages and living expenses with RFA; the other is a family with middle school and primary school children who detailed their household expenditures. All wages, prices, and expenditure details cited in the article are based on facts confirmed in those interviews. Mr. Kim and Ms. Lee are pseudonyms.

Last month’s take-home pay for Mr. Kim – a 45-year old man who works a government-assigned job in a state-run food processing plant in South Pyongan province – was 20,000 won (about 30 US cents). Although his official wage is set at 50,000 won a month, 30,000 won was deducted upfront as “social support” for state construction projects, education funds, and agricultural supply purchases.
Because production levels and management vary widely across industries and state enterprises in North Korea, worker compensation differs significantly. While well-managed, profitable factories pay higher wages, struggling facilities cannot guarantee even baseline monthly compensation.
Mr. Kim was fortunate to receive any pay at all this month – raw materials arrived on time, keeping his factory’s assembly line running. Workers at other plants were not as lucky. They received nothing when supply shortages ground operations to a halt.
Even though he is one of the lucky ones who got paid, a 20,000-won income cannot buy a single kilogram (2.2 pounds) of white rice – currently priced at over 40,000 won per kilogram – or even a kilogram of corn, which costs around 25,000 won.
Based on October price and wage data verified through sources inside North Korea, RFA compiled a monthly budget for a composite four-member household—comprising factory worker Mr. Kim, his wife Ms. Lee, and their two school-aged children—to illustrate the reality of monthly living expenses.
The reported commodity prices were gathered from South and North Pyongan, South and North Hwanghae, and Kangwon provinces.
A simulated November household budget for a fictional family of four in North Korea shows a monthly deficit of about 1.3 million won (about $18), based on October prices in southern North Korea reported by RFA sources.
(RFA Korean) Starting each month ‘in the red’
With two children attending school, the Kim household budget starts in the red every month.
Schools demand children bring “assignment quotas” of waste paper and scrap metal for recycling – it is a mandatory patriotic offering. Collecting the materials takes a lot of time and effort, so most students pay in cash instead – to the tune of around 30,000 won per month. With two kids, that’s 60,000 won, already triple Mr. Kim’s salary.
On top of that, home utilities cost roughly 5,000 won per month. Even though water and electricity can and do cut out at any given moment, they still have to pay the bill.
Thus the Kim family is already 45,000 won in the hole before factoring in the cost of food.
In some factories, 5 to 10 kilograms (about 10-20 pounds) of corn is said to be supplied to working employees once a month, while in North Hamgyong Province, the rice or prepared food items that were previously provided have been completely cut off. Circumstances differ depending on the region, factory, and enterprise, but at any rate, what families are provided through their workplaces is a mere fraction of what they need to eat each month.
According to the daily food recommendations set by North Korean authorities – 750 grams of corn for workers, 550 grams for housewives and 450 grams for students, the monthly food requirement based on three meals per day for the Kims is about 66 kilograms.
1.65 million won corn deficit. Rice? Keep dreaming
How much money does the Kim family need just to scrape by each month?
According to sources, as of October, the price of white rice traded in North and South Pyongan provinces is about 40,000 won per kilogram, and corn is around 25,000 won. In North Hamgyong and Ryanggang provinces, 1 kilogram of white rice has already exceeded 50,000 won.
If the family relied entirely on white rice, their monthly food bill would reach 2.64 million won—equivalent to 52 months of Mr. Kim’s nominal salary of 50,000 won. Rice is therefore a luxury that only the wealthiest North Koreans can afford. Like most North Koreans, the Kims will get by on a diet of mostly corn. A monthly supply costs a total 1.65 million won, which is 33 times Mr. Kim’s nominal monthly income.
Workers at the Ryuwon footwear factory produce various types of Ryuwon-trademarked shoes in Pyongyang, North Korea, Sept. 25, 2020.
(Jon Chol Jin/AP) Jiro Ishimaru, head of the Osaka-based ASIAPRESS media outlet that covers North Korea, explained, “Currently, with a North Korean worker’s salary, rice is out of the question, and they barely live centered around corn.” Asiapress tracks commodity and food prices in various regions through its contacts in North Korea.
“ In the case of working at a state enterprise, it varies by rank and industry, but roughly the monthly pay provided by the state is between 35,000 won and 100,000 won,” he said. “Even if a well-performing state enterprise pays double the salary at 200,000 won, with that money you cannot even buy 5 kilograms of white rice, and there is no such thing as rations. With such wages, people are barely able to live on a diet centered on corn.”
Under these constraints, balanced meals with adequate protein remain an unaffordable luxury. Pork sells for 270,000 won per kilogram—more than 13 times Mr. Kim’s take-home wage – pollack costs 100,000 won per kilogram, and eggs sell for 10,000 won each.
Other important food-related items are also out of reach. Bottled water runs between 5,000 and 10,000 won per liter, and a 10-liter container of imported Russian cooking oil costs 200,000 to 250,000 won. Although prices vary by quality and region, such items remain entirely unattainable on a 20,000-won salary.
Adding basic daily necessities, staple food supplies like condiments, and transportation expenses, the growing deficit is only made worse when unexpected expenses arise.
So the family somehow needs to earn more money to get by.
Side hustles to feed the family
Like most other families, the Kims need side hustles to bridge the gap between Mr. Kim’s income and their monthly living costs. Ms. Lee used to trade goods in the marketplace to earn money, but then the government started cracking down on informal market activity. Now she has turned to day labor, hauling heavy loads or doing manual labor at construction sites. According to sources, the daily wages people earn from this sort of work can be about 100,000 - 200,000 won. In one day of manual labor, she earns double what her husband earns working a full month at the factory.
However, informal work is irregular. Even if Ms. Lee secures 15 days of labor a month and brings in 1.5 million won, her earnings still fall short of covering the 1.65 million won needed just to buy monthly corn supplies.
Ishimaru explained that there are other types of jobs that people can get to bridge the gap.
“Since official salaries alone are not enough, as all our contacts tell us now, assembling products at home—like wigs or eyelashes—serve as side jobs,” said Ishimaru. .
In October 2023, when North Korean authorities drastically increased the legal monthly wages of state enterprise workers, office staff, and civil servants by at least 10 to over 20 times, most North Korean residents welcomed it. Expectations were high that they could eat three meals a day and enjoy basic living, but in just 3 to 4 years, massive inflation caused by shortages, and currency devaluation hit the public economy hard.
RFA sources reported that most workers do not expect wages to serve as a means of livelihood, pointing out the severe gap between state-fixed wages and individual day labor. They criticized North Korea as “socialist in appearance, but more capitalist than actual capitalism.”
Winter brings high coal costs
In November, an even bigger crisis is facing the Kim household: heat. Coal prices have skyrocketed to 800,000–900,000 won per metric ton, more than quadruple the cost just six years ago.
In North Korea, a four-member household usually needs at minimum 1 to 1.5 metric tons of coal to get through winter. To actually be warm, they need at least 3 metric tons, but the Kims decided to stick to minimal heating. Preparing firewood for the winter should have started back in the summer, but Mr. Kim, burdened with monthly budget deficits and struggling just to put food on the table, had no time to spare.
North Korea's Kaephung county is seen from the observatory of the Aegibong Peace Ecopark in Gimpo, South Korea, Nov. 29, 2024.
(Lee Jin-man/AP) Families must also prepare food supplies to get them through the winter, and this has traditionally been done through kimjang, where families gather together and make large amounts of kimchi – enough to last through the colder half of the year.
Sources told RFA that the vegetables that go into kimchi are expensive: napa cabbage currently costs 9,000 to 10,000 won per kilogram, while radishes cost 7,000 to 8,000 won per kilogram. While a family of four typically needs around 300 kilograms of cabbage for the season, the Kim household plans to prepare a minimal batch of 30 kilograms of cabbage kimchi and 10 kilograms of radish kimchi without extra seasonings. Even this reduced batch costs at least 340,000 won, driving the family deeper into debt.
Sources estimate that a four-person household in North Korea needs approximately $80 to $100 USD (roughly 5.9 million to 7.8 million North Korean won) per month for baseline survival, yet ordinary residents operate on less than half that amount. Even if Ms. Lee works day labor and side jobs all month to earn 3 million won, the family still reaches only half of the required subsistence threshold.
RFA asked Ishimaru how ordinary North Korean families manage to survive under persistent deficits.
“I’m really curious too. Truly curious,” Ishimaru said. “Residents in provincial cities live under very difficult conditions. Everyone assesses that life was much more comfortable before 2019, … when individual economic activities were possible.”
To make matters worse, sources project that as usual, grain prices will rise again starting in December as the worst months of winter roll in. Mr. Kim will continue working at the factory to receive 20,000 won. To cover the deficit budget of their 4-member family, his wife Ms. Lee will have to find unofficial work at 100,000 won a day for at least half the month of December to make ends meet, even on their family’s tightened budget.
Edited by Noh Jung Min in Korean and by Charlie Dharapak and Eugene Whong in English.

articles.title: The Download: Pelosi’s successor targets AI and data centers face power woes
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in…
articles.fullText:
This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

—Grace Huckins

As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

I spoke with Wiener only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk: during our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times.

“We need to slow this down,” he told me. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Still, he describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI. Here’s what he plans to do about it .

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

—James O’Donnell

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash sweeping the country arguably first began to take shape.

Big Tech has framed the data center uproar as a culture war over progress. But a few days in Ashburn convinced me the real fault line may be electricity: drawing it from the grid or generating it onsite provokes different forms of blowback.

The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Find out why .

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair
But Trump says he doesn’t think Huang needs to worry. ( AP News )
+ Huang hired a PR firm known for handling sex scandals last year. ( Wired $)
+ The allegations will likely spur new chip export restrictions. ( Reuters $)
+ They also raise questions about Huang’s lobbying on China. ( Verge )
+ And threaten the fate of the economy. ( WP $)

2 France has accused Iran of hacking its supermarket fridges
Prosecutors are investigating the leaders of an Iranian cyber unit. ( NPR )
+ Hackers are shifting to manipulating physical equipment. ( Axios )
+ Is your smart kitchen next? ( Wired $)

3 The Iran war has triggered a drop in global emissions
The main driver is energy supply constraints. ( New Scientist $)

articles.title: Evolving metal extraction processes
articles.excerpt: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting…
articles.fullText:
The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.

Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”

A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.

Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.

Beyond optimization

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.

Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology

Source : Outokumpu

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.

Innovation happens at the boundaries

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.

Building a technology platform

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.

“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.

That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.

The future of materials companies

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO 2 , chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.

The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?

The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

Read more about this topic and hear more from Caspar Stinn and Antoine Allanore .

This content was produced by Outokumpu. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

articles.title: No internet, no advance warning: 11 killed in Myanmar military bombing in Sagaing
articles.excerpt: Civilians in war zones are left vulnerable as Starlink internet becomes scarce after scam center crackdown.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Burmese
It was just before noon on Saturday. Three gyrocopters flew low as they approached Nyaung Pin Lay village. A school and surrounding residential area was bombed. Eleven were killed, including four children.
A resident told RFA that although the local People’s Defense Forces (PDF) received a tip that the Myanmar military would bomb the school, the warning could not reach them in time due to the lack of internet in the village.
“Information that this would be bombed was sent online to everyone. They did inform us,” the Kani Township resident told RFA on the condition of anonymity for security reasons.
“But because there was no Starlink communication, casualties were high as a result. About a month ago in Nat La Po village, when we got the exact location that would be bombed and cleared the area, there were no casualties. That was fortunate. But now, even though we got the location to be bombed, communication was cut off.”
A May 25, 2025, photo shows a Starlink sign at an internet cafe in Demoso, Myanmar.
(AFP) In Myanmar, home to the world’s longest-running civil war, the military-appointed government has cut off phone lines and internet communications in over 40 percent of townships nationwide. Locals, civil society groups, and revolutionary forces tell RFA that they rely on Starlink — acquiring the devices through unofficial and often expensive channels — as a lifeline for information.
In October 2025, SpaceX announced the disabling of over 2,500 Starlink kits in Myanmar to crack down on transnational cyber-scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border. Subsequent restrictions by SpaceX on unregistered units bought outside of Myanmar have shut down countless others.
Since June, more than 20 percent of Starlink internet devices used in Myanmar have had their services cut off, according to a report released on Oct. 23 by the group Athan.
Local residents and human rights activists told RFA that this has created a crisis for the survival of civilians in areas of intense civil conflict.
A Myanmar government photo taken on Oct. 20, 2025, shows seized Starlink devices during a raid on the KK Park online scam center in Myawaddy.
(Myanmar Military Information Team via AFP) “The military cutting off phone lines and internet connections from the start was intentionally aimed at concealing human rights violations they commit and restricting people’s freedom of expression,” said Joy, a research director at Athan, a non-profit organization for the Freedom of Expression Movement in Myanmar.
“If Starlink also stops providing services to Myanmar and cuts connections, emergency humanitarian aid, air strike alerts, news regarding military columns, and natural disaster warnings for these local residents will stop immediately.”
According to a report titled “Dead Air” released by Athan on October 23, the communication cut-off directly affects the lives and safety of people in conflict-affected regions as they can no longer receive warnings about airstrikes and military movements, medical aid, or updates on family members’ safety and evacuation routes.
RFA contacted Khaing Khaing Soe, spokesperson for the military-appointed president’s office, regarding when internet and phone lines might be restored. She instead referred RFA to the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications.
Now, not only Starlink devices used by scam operations are being shut down, but Starlink connections used by civilians have also been suspended starting in June this year, with more than 20 percent of devices cut off by October, according to Athan. Consequently, regions like Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, Rakhine, Kayah State, and other areas experiencing severe conflict were directly affected, Athan’s report states.
RFA contacted SpaceX regarding the impact on civilians in regions where the internet has been cut off, but has not received a response at the time of publication.
“Some of our Starlink devices were disabled. This has caused a lot of trouble for us,” said Aye Myint Aung Aung, Head of the Department of Humanitarian Assistance and Emergency Management under the Mandalay Regional Interim Administrative Council.
“On the other hand, whether it’s our civilians, revolutionary groups, or those leading and operating the administrative mechanism in revolutionary forces, everyone relies on Starlink. As access to information becomes more restricted, limitations on civilian safety also increase. I would define this as a very major challenge for us.”
In Kayah State, Deputy Minister of Defense for the Karenni State Government Khu Daniel told RFA that Starlink connections are being shut down one by one, raising concerns.
“For the public and for the youth currently fighting in battle, it will become a cause for concern,” he said.
A Sept. 17, 2025, photo shows people on a balcony of a building with what appears to be Starlink satellite dishes on the roof in the KK Park complex in Myawaddy, Myanmar.
(Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP) Khun Chit Htoo, who is assisting refugees in the Karenni Region, said that if all Starlink services are shut down, it could have a severe impact on humanitarian aid operations.
“Our current work relies on internet connectivity as well as donors. Since we connect online, we are very concerned,” said Khun Chit Htoo.
“We will face a situation where we can no longer help needy civilians receive the support they really need across all aspects of coordination. If there is no internet line left, I believe we stand to lose a lot because of this single connection.”
While welcoming and supporting the shutdown of Starlink internet lines used by online scam operations to crack down on scam syndicates, 317 civil society organizations issued a statement on July 17 expressing deep concern over potential negative impacts if all Starlink terminals nationwide are shut down.
According to an October 23 report by the Myanmar Internet Project, an organization monitoring internet shutdowns and conflicts, there were 581 military airstrikes that killed at least 353 civilians in the three months from July to September 2026, with 562 of those attacks occurring in areas where internet service was cut off.
Translated by Nayrein Kyaw. Edited by Charlie Dharapak.

articles.title: A trip to the South Korean seaside for glimpses of my North Korean hometown
articles.excerpt: Escapee Park Sol-ji often gets homesick for the port city of Chongjin. A beach day in Busan comes close.
articles.fullText:
Read a version of this story in Korean .
Park Sol-ji stared out over the water at Gwangalli Beach with the iconic Gwangan Bridge in the distance, just above the horizon. South Korea’s touristy second largest city of Busan is a drastic change from heavily industrialized Chongjin – her hometown in North Korea. But both cities are large ports on the eastern side of the peninsula, and the sand, the breeze, and the smell of the sea reminds her of home.
“I love looking at the sea, and coming here whenever I miss my hometown is a big part of it,” she told Radio Free Asia Nov. 3. “Also, coming to the seaside makes me feel like I can finally breathe. I think I like it because it gives me such a sense of liberation.”
Park Sol-ji is a pseudonym she is using for safety reasons. Sol-ji fled North Korea 19 years ago when she was 20 years old, arriving in South Korea the following year. Adjusting to life in the fast-paced South was jarring. Though she tried her best to blend in among South Korean 20-somethings , it would all come crashing down whenever she spoke with her unmistakable North Korean accent.
She often found the degree of change in her life to be overwhelming, and she longed to return home, but that was now impossible. In times like that a trip to the sea would always remind her just enough of home to boost her spirits.
These days, she’s shed the accent and looks about the same as everyone else, but she still gets homesick and often travels to the seaside.
A map showing the locations of Chongjin, North Korea and Busan, South Korea.
(RFA) Busan is very different from Chongjin. Though both cities are industrialized ports, the South Korean city has – over many decades – invested in travel infrastructure and branded itself as a global tourist destination.
According to tourism statistics compiled by the Busan city government, more than 3.93 million foreign tourists have already visited Busan this year alone. CNN introduced Busan as “Asia’s Next Coastal City,” and Expedia selected Busan as the only Korean destination among its “Top 10 Destinations of the Year for 2027.”
But for Sol-ji, it’s not the glitz and glamor she’s coming for. She is here to take in the memories of the seaside of her childhood, where she played in the sand with her friends and spent precious moments with her family.
Memories roll in with the rising tide
Though the forecast called for cloudy weather, Gwangalli Beach had quite a few visitors from midday, perhaps due to the unexpectedly clear sky. Couples were taking photos with the sea as a backdrop, groups of noisy students on a field trip made their way across the sand, and foreign tourists walked barefoot. Everyone had smiles on their faces. Gwangalli Beach is well known as a romantic spot where the blue sea harmonizes with the spectacular night view of the Gwangan Bridge.
Sol-ji slowly surveyed the seascape and her face lit up as she spoke of the days she and her family would break out a large cauldron, build a fire, catch fish, and cook eojuk, a type of spicy fish porridge. She also remembered how she and her friends used to play by pulling up seaweed to gather in makeshift nets made of their extra clothes. Although these were ordinary childhood games, looking back now, they were moments she can never have again. To her, the sea is a landscape she longs for, as well as a place where she finds solace for her wounds.
“I even dreamt of returning to Chongjin because I missed my hometown, but even in the dream, seeing my dyed hair and decorated nails, I thought I would get caught,” she said. North Korea is notorious for fashion police who crack down on “capitalist” looks like dyed hair, colored nails, blue jeans, clothing with English words and phrases, and other no-nos. In South Korea, Sol-ji is free to dress how she wants to, but that does not erase her longing.
“I really do want to go back just once.”
The old village in the hills
Prior to visiting the beach, Sol-ji had started the day with a train ride to Busan Station, disembarking in the morning. The first spot on her itinerary was Gamcheon Culture Village, a 10-minute taxi ride away. The village started as a ramshackle town built up in the hills for laborers, and it expanded greatly with the swell of refugees fleeing to Busan from the advancing North Korean army in the opening weeks of the 1950-53 Korean War. In recent years the village was painstakingly restored through cultural preservation and beautification projects.
These days, tourists flock to its narrow meandering streets, attracted by the colorfully painted houses, many of which have been converted to shops, cafes and mini-museums. Near the high point of the village sits a colorful statue of the Little Prince, presiding over a space dedicated to the mythos presented in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s world-renowned novella.
A statue of the Little Prince and the fox at the Little Prince House in Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea.
(Saha-gu Office via korea.net) Today, the tourists have come in force. More often than not, passersby who came for the village’s unique artsy flair will be speaking in a language other than Korean.
While most tourists are browsing the shops, ordering refreshments, or taking in one of the museums, Sol-ji slowly looks around the alley, finally focusing on a clothesline in the courtyard of one house. She noticed three or four items of clothing hanging on a single line, swaying in the breeze. It was this evidence that people actually live here that conjured up the feelings of her childhood.
“People here hang their laundry on clotheslines like that. It’s exactly the same in North Korea,” she said. She explained that in North Korea some families have washing machines, but rolling blackouts are common in most places, so people still have to do laundry by hand.
“So here they also dry their laundry in the sun,” she said. “Knowing this is quite heartwarming.”
In another area of town she operated a manual pump that once drew water out of the ground. She said it made her think of her grandmother’s house in Chongjin.
Sol-ji walked along, looking around every corner of the alley. Though sun-dried laundry and the hand pump might be similar details, the nature of this town, built up on a hillside, would never make sense in Chongjin, she said.
Park Sol-ji, visits Gamcheon Culture Village in Busan, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026.
